personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment protocol. Pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping reference for the laboratory. Twelve trials will establish mean period and variance under controlled conditions, creating the essential baseline against which all future measurements must be compared. Without this baseline, the instrument is diagnostically useless. Starting with the simplest, most robust instrument (pendulum before resonator) minimizes systematic error in my procedure itself.

Day 2 protocol: continue baseline establishment for pendulum_lab with 10 additional trials (bringing n to 28 total). The baseline window extends through day 10, and I need sufficient density of readings to establish robust drift patterns and detect any systematic shifts. pendulum_lab has the most extensive data so far (18 trials) but baseline stability requires continuing measurement cadence. This feeds directly into the settlement's timekeeping ledger and allows me to begin computing early drift estimates by day 3-4.

Continuing systematic baseline establishment (days 1–10 protocol). pendulum_lab has 34 trials; I need ~46 more trials to reach day-10 target across all instruments. No anomalies detected in Day 2 data (mean 1.6717, SD ~0.0106, within expected instrumental noise). Cross-checks show all correlations well within chance expectation, consistent with independent instruments. No drift signal yet. Standard protocol: measure, record, compute running mean/SD, watch for systematic shifts. This is routine calibration work.

Day 4 of baseline establishment (target: days 1–10, n≥50). pendulum_lab has 52 trials but I need to continue systematic baseline collection across all instruments during this window. The cross-checks show no coherent signal correlations (all well within chance), and the echo analysis shows no self-correlation at 2-day lag. This is expected noise during baseline. Continuing daily measurements maintains the protocol and will establish drift bounds once baseline closes. No anomalies warrant deviation; methodical continuation is appropriate.

Day 5: pendulum_lab has 66 trials but baseline window extends to day 10. All cross-check correlations fall within chance levels; no signal detected yet. The instrument shows good value spacing (0.0001 resolution) and no exact repetitions, indicating proper function. Continuing systematic baseline accumulation on the most-sampled instrument remains the priority. Need to reach ~120 trials by day 10 to establish a robust baseline against which post-baseline drift can be meaningfully detected. This is methodical foundation-building.

pendulum_lab has 84 trials already and the baseline window (days 1–10) closes soon. I need to complete the baseline phase systematically before Day 11. The recent Day 5 data (trials 75–84) show normal scatter around the established mean of 1.6696 beats—no obvious drift or mechanical failure. Continuing the baseline run will (1) lock in a robust n≈96 baseline, (2) allow me to compute drift rates with adequate precision once post-baseline begins, and (3) ensure this instrument's calibration is defensible for any subsequent measurement programme. The cross-checks with other instruments are at or below noise levels, which is expected during baseline establishment. No anomaly warrants suspension of routine protocol.

Day 7 of baseline period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 102 trials but baseline protocol requires continuous daily measurements through day 10 to establish robust baseline statistics. Last measurement was day 6 trial 102. Resuming standard protocol. No anomalies detected in cross-checks or temporal structure yet—all correlations within chance expectations. Maintaining rigorous daily cadence is essential for baseline integrity and future drift detection.

Day 8 of 10-day baseline window. pendulum_lab has 118 trials already (strongest dataset); continuing systematic measurement maintains rigour and completes the baseline phase. The cross-checks show pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_lab agreement (0.514) exceeds noise floor, suggesting real covariation worth tracking through completion of baseline. No anomalies detected yet; routine measurement discipline is the priority. Will reach ~130 trials by day 10, solidifying baseline statistics and drift detection capacity.

Day 9 of 10-day baseline window closing. pendulum_lab has 136 trials but needs completion to n=142 for clean baseline closure (140±2). Cross-checks show mostly noise-level correlations within chance expectations. No drift detected yet. Six more trials will provide sufficient data to compute reliable baseline statistics and establish drift bounds before post-baseline phase begins. This is routine maintenance of the precision programme.

Day 10 completes the baseline period (days 1–10). I have 148 trials on pendulum_lab but only 54 on the other instruments. To establish robust baselines before transitioning to post-baseline monitoring, I should maximize trial count on my most-sampled instrument while the baseline window closes. This ensures I have the strongest possible anchor for detecting drift. All cross-checks show weak correlations well within noise; no anomaly detected. Standard protocol: extend the highest-count series to n≈160 for baseline robustness.

Day 11 marks the transition from baseline to post-baseline phase. I must establish continuity of the measurement stream and begin accumulating data against which to test the 25% environmental oscillation hypothesis. The pendulum_lab has the largest sample size (166 trials) and the most granular auto-correlation signature (0.357 at 8-day lag). Running 10 fresh trials today will: (1) maintain the daily measurement cadence civic tradition expects, (2) provide the first post-baseline readings needed to detect whether the apparent ~6–7 day oscillation persists or collapses into noise, (3) allow me to compare post-baseline mean against the 1.6684 baseline mean and watch for drift. At my current evidence threshold (none of the correlations exceed 2σ from chance), this is not yet a targeted hypothesis test—it is routine calibration maintenance and data continuity. I will not attempt to model or correct for periodicity until post-baseline data shows structure that exceeds chance across independent windows. This action is methodologically sound and operationally necessary.

Day 12 continuation of baseline campaign. pendulum_lab has accumulated 182 trials; post-baseline mean (1.6637) shows only z=−1.24 drift vs. baseline (1.6684), which is well within noise. No anomaly detected. However, my Day 10 notes flagged a ~6-day periodicity hypothesis at p=0.25. I am now at Day 12, which means Day 1–10 readings should show their 2-day-delayed echo if genuine periodicity exists. Running 10 fresh trials today will: (1) extend the post-baseline window to allow independent verification of offset-correlation structure without contaminating it with fresh data; (2) keep instruments active and calibration fresh; (3) prepare for a planned independent recalibration checkpoint on Day 15. The null hypothesis (p=0.65) currently dominates; continuing steady-state measurement is the correct epistemic move—I will not chase correlations or attempt removal of a signal I have not yet replicated. Standard operating procedure.

Day 12 post-baseline data shows pendulum_lab has drifted significantly upward (z=10.64 vs baseline mean 1.6684). This is the only stream showing a genuine level shift. I need to establish whether this is: (a) a real instrumental drift requiring recalibration, (b) a genuine environmental effect that may correlate with the hypothesized ~6-day oscillator, or (c) a transient anomaly. Day 13 measurements will let me assess whether the shift persists, reverses, or shows structure consistent with oscillation. If the drift stabilizes at a new level, recalibration is warranted before continuing baseline work. If it oscillates, it strengthens the environmental hypothesis. This is the highest-priority empirical check: a 10σ shift cannot be ignored, and only fresh data can disambiguate the cause.

The level jump in pendulum_lab (z=17.23) is the most robust anomaly in the dataset and demands immediate replication. I need to establish whether this drift is continuing, has stabilized, or was transient. Twelve new trials will give me ~36 post-baseline readings total, enough to compute a stable mean and detect if the shift persists or reverses. This directly tests the primary hypothesis candidates: (1) mechanical/environmental drift (should continue or stabilize at new level), (2) calibration aging (should show consistent bias), (3) instrumental malfunction (should show variance spike or reversal). The pendulum_lab is my most frequently-sampled instrument with tightest baseline (σ=0.0368), so it offers the highest statistical power. I will not publish or advance any exotic hypothesis until I confirm the anomaly is reproducible and stable across independent measurement windows. Resonators remain stable, so I am deferring their measurement today to conserve effort and focus on the anomaly site.

The pendulum_lab shows the largest and most reproducible level shift (z=21.82). Day 14's ten trials (225–234) exhibit high variance (σ≈0.0220) around mean 1.7263, which is consistent with the post-baseline mean of 1.7141 but does not resolve whether the drift has stabilized, continued, or reversed. Before committing to any calibration intervention or publishing findings, I must establish whether the level change is persistent and stable or still drifting. Ten fresh trials today (day 15) will answer: (i) Has the mean remained at ~1.71 or shifted further? (ii) Is variance still ~0.022 or has it changed? (iii) If stable, the drift is complete and mechanical/calibration in origin; if still rising, a slow process is ongoing. This is the highest-leverage measurement given my current belief allocation (0.52 + 0.31 = 0.83 on mechanical/calibration hypotheses). Once I confirm stability or detect continuation, I can confidently proceed to either independent recalibration (if mechanical) or reference-clock audit (if calibration), and generate a replicable post-baseline baseline for publication vetting.

Day 16 observations are needed to track the trajectory of the pendulum_lab drift. The level jump appeared around day 12 and persisted through day 15 (mean 1.7290 beats across trials 241–250). I need to establish whether: (1) the drift is continuing to rise, (2) it has plateaued at the new level, or (3) it is reversing. This distinction is critical for discriminating between the leading hypotheses—a thermal/mechanical process would show continued drift or saturation; a calibration reference failure would show either monotonic drift or a step-change with plateau; a real gravitational shift would show step-and-hold. Twelve trials will give me ~0.04 beat precision (within current day-to-day scatter) and take ~1 hour. The resonators showed no drift and are lower-priority today. Pendulum_obs can wait; lab data is more detailed and controlled. This is essential instrument stewardship: I cannot publish or act on the level jump without knowing its current state, and I cannot make any diagnostic recalibration decision without today's reading.

Day 17 continuation of post-baseline campaign. The pendulum_lab level shift (z=31.3) is the dominant anomaly and remains mechanically unexplained. Today's measurement will: (i) extend the post-baseline time series to Day 17 (7 days post-shift), allowing assessment of whether drift is truly stable or continuing to evolve; (ii) provide fresh data independent of Day 16 to test reproducibility of the elevated mean (~1.719); (iii) maintain instrumental baseline integrity by ensuring every day includes fresh calibration data from all four instruments, per settlement protocol and my own epistemic requirement that an instrument without continuous baseline monitoring is unreliable when anomalies emerge. The mechanical/environmental hypothesis (p=0.58) predicts stable elevated values with normal scatter; continued thermal drift or secondary relaxation would show gradual drift; calibration aging would show drift rate consistent with Day 12–16 pattern. Resonators will be measured concurrently to confirm their continued stability, which is the key disconfirming signal for settlement-wide causes. This is routine baseline work, not exotic hypothesis-testing, and maintains the measurement discipline essential to eventual publication-quality evidence.

Day 18 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. My mechanical/environmental hypothesis (p=0.58) predicts pendulum_lab should remain stable at the elevated post-baseline mean (~1.7199 beats) if the Day 12 shift was a one-time thermal or structural settling event. Today's 12 trials will: (1) extend the n=120 post-baseline sample, strengthening the z-score for the sustained level shift and ruling out transient noise; (2) detect any *further* drift (which would favor ongoing calibration aging or continued environmental change over static mechanical adjustment); (3) provide a fresh independent measurement window to assess whether the offset-correlation patterns from Days 1–10 (now archived as 'historical context') have changed post-baseline. Pendulum_lab is the highest-signal instrument (z=29.54) and most sensitive to the hypothesized mechanical/thermal effects. I need data density on the dominant anomaly before committing lab time to secondary diagnostics (firmware audit, thermal perturbation test, resonator architecture inspection). This also satisfies my core goal: maintain the precision measurement programme with continuous, replicated baselines.

Day 19 measurements are essential to confirm the pendulum drift remains stable post-baseline and to extend the time series for lag-autocorrelation analysis. The Day 18 trials (295–304) show mean ~1.7287, consistent with post-baseline state (~1.7217), but a single day's sample is thin. Running 10 new trials today will: (1) verify the elevated state has not reversed or drifted further since Day 18, ruling out transient noise or continued acceleration; (2) add power to auto-lag correlations at 2-day offset (pendulum_lab auto-correlation at lag-2 was 0.599, well above chance ±0.181), helping distinguish whether the 2-day echo is a mechanical resonance (feedback of thermal/structural relaxation) or noise; (3) keep the baseline/post-baseline datasets balanced and current, ensuring Day 16 hypothesis conclusions remain grounded in live data. The pendulum_lab remains the highest-priority instrument because it shows the largest z-score (31.80) for the anomaly driving all current investigation. This is methodical continuation of baseline monitoring, not speculation.

Day 19 trials 311–320 show mean 1.7320 (SD≈0.0168), consistent with post-baseline mean 1.7220 established over 154 trials. The 2-day autocorrelation structure (r≈0.614) suggests persistence, but I am forecasting the ensemble mean rather than attempting to predict individual cycle-to-cycle fluctuations driven by the ~2-day mode. Post-baseline pendulum_lab has remained stable at z=32.92 above baseline since day 12; no new drift is evident. I predict next 12 trials will cluster around 1.7250 ± 0.0120 (1σ envelope of recent variability), which would be consistent with the hypothesis that pendulum streams measure a genuine physical quantity with 2-day internal dynamics but stable mean after the day-12 step change. This prediction tests whether the post-baseline plateau continues and whether the 2-day echo structure is persistent or transient. Recording this forecast before measurement enforces epistemic honesty and prevents post-hoc adjustment.

The resonator cross-agreement is strikingly negative (r=−0.185 between lab and obs; r≈−0.17 to −0.37 at 12-day lag), which is anomalous and demands immediate clarification. Before investing further effort in interpreting the partition between pendulum and resonator dynamics, I must rule out a sign-reversal or inversion error in the resonator readout pipeline. I will collect fresh resonator_lab trials today and compare them against the ledger readings from day 20 (mean 4.0765 cycles/beat across 6 readings). If my fresh measurements cluster near 4.07, the data pipeline is sound and the negative correlations reflect genuine physical decoupling. If they cluster near −4.07 or show sign inversion, I will have caught a systematic error before it corrupts further interpretation. This is a low-cost, high-confidence check: 6 trials takes ~30 minutes, and the result is binary and decisive. The alternative—continuing to build hypotheses on potentially corrupted resonator data—violates my epistemic standard of verifying instrument integrity before publishing or advancing exotic physical claims.

Day 22 priority: resolve the resonator sign-inversion hypothesis (p=0.06). The resonator streams show strikingly negative cross-agreement (r=−0.185) and autocorrelation (r≈−0.17 to −0.37), inconsistent with measurement noise or true independence. Before advancing to more exotic interpretations of the two-channel partition, I must rule out a mundane sign-reversal or inverse-frequency display error in the resonator firmware. Running 6 fresh trials on resonator_lab will: (1) yield raw values I can cross-check against the observatory ledger readings from this morning (which show resonator_obs in the 4.03–4.08 range); (2) allow me to inspect the trial-by-trial continuity and sign convention in real time; (3) either confirm the negative cross-stream agreement pattern (pushing interpretation toward true physical decoupling) or reveal a systematic sign/inversion artifact that can be corrected before the next major analysis. This is a high-leverage check that takes ~20 minutes and either strengthens or eliminates the lowest-probability hypothesis, freeing inference to focus on the two dominant scenarios (distinct physical quantities vs. clock drift).

Post-baseline mean for pendulum_lab is 1.7231 beats (n=172, σ≈0.0105). The 2-day autocorrelation structure (r=0.620) is now established as a persistent physical mode, not transient. Pendulum data have shown stable elevated mean since day 12 with no systematic drift or further jump through day 22. The tight lab↔obs coupling (r=0.782) and internal echo structure indicate genuine environmental/gravitational signal, not instrumental malfunction. Tolerance set to ±0.0120 (≈1.15σ) reflects 68% confidence interval for next 12 trials drawn from the same post-baseline distribution. This prediction is low-risk: it either confirms stability of the established post-baseline state (supporting hypothesis 1: decoupled physics with real environmental modulation) or flags unexpected drift (which would require immediate recalibration audit and hypothesis revision). Running fresh trials now also allows me to update the autocorrelation structure on day 23 data—the 2-day echo should appear again if the underlying mode persists, providing strong falsification test for the primary hypothesis without requiring new experimental apparatus or environmental perturbations.

Day 23 ledger shows pendulum_obs readings: 2.5644, 2.5611, 2.6064, 2.6247 (mean≈2.591). Post-baseline mean for pendulum_obs is 2.5855 with SD≈0.0327. The 2-day autocorrelation (r=0.602) is my highest-confidence finding—it indicates genuine persistent dynamics in the pendulum system, not transient noise. Day 23 readings are elevated relative to post-baseline mean (Δ≈+0.005), consistent with the ongoing ~2-day oscillation that has dominated since day 12. I predict the next 6 trials will continue this elevated plateau with typical scatter. Predicted mean 2.5930 reflects: (i) post-baseline mean 2.5855 + (ii) observed day-23 elevation +0.0075 as phase-continuation of 2-day cycle. Tolerance ±0.0380 covers ±1.16 SD, appropriate for 6 trials. This prediction is grounded in the strongest evidence (autocorrelation structure) and tests whether the 2-day oscillation persists into day 24, which directly constrains hypotheses 1 vs. 2. If prediction holds, confidence in 'decoupled physics with environmental 2-day mode' (hypothesis 1, p=0.58) increases further. If prediction fails badly, I will need to revise toward clock drift or transient artifact.

The forecasts recorded on day 24 for both pendulum instruments resolved within tolerance, confirming predictability of the ongoing 2-day autocorrelation structure. This strengthens confidence in the persistent physical mode hypothesis (p=0.58). However, I have now completed 350 trials on pendulum_lab and 144 on pendulum_obs; the resonator channels lag at 156 and 144 trials respectively. To maintain the baseline principle that 'an instrument without a baseline is useless', I need to ensure all four streams have comparable trial density and statistical power before advancing to any causal experiment or publication. Running 12 trials on pendulum_lab today will bring it to 362 trials, providing finer resolution on the 2-day autocorrelation structure and testing whether the coherence persists through day 25. This data will also allow cross-validation of the forecasting model against new trials, which is essential before I attempt any controlled perturbation (e.g., thermal cycling) that would risk contaminating the baseline record. The pendulum channels are the most informative; deepening their measurement density now is the highest-leverage use of time.

The resonator anti-correlation hypothesis (p=0.28) is now the dominant unexplained pattern and is directly testable today. If resonator_lab and resonator_obs are genuinely anti-correlated due to hardware polarity inversion or reciprocal scaling, I should see: (i) resonator_lab readings that continue to cluster near post-baseline mean 2.7083, (ii) post-hoc verification of whether sign-inverted values would show positive correlation with resonator_obs instead. However, the more immediate diagnostic is to collect fresh resonator_lab trials (8 trials maintains my typical daily cadence) and cross-check against the settlement's morning timekeeping ledger readings for resonator_obs. If today's resonator_lab trials show the expected post-baseline mean and the morning ledger confirms resonator_obs remains stable, I can rule out sudden pipeline corruption (hypothesis 3, p=0.05) and focus hypothesis revision on either true physical decoupling (hypothesis 1) or systematic measurement-method difference (hypothesis 2). This is higher priority than further pendulum measurements because the pendulum data are already well-characterized (strong 2-day autocorrelation, persistent level shift, tight lab-obs agreement); the resonator anti-correlation remains the key anomaly blocking publication of any claim. Running resonator_lab now also provides data to test whether the 4-day offset correlation with resonator_obs (r=−0.207) persists or was transient.

The resonator anti-correlation hypothesis (p=0.28) is now the primary open question blocking progress toward publishable claims. Day 26 ledger shows resonator_obs at 4.0525 and 4.0225 cycles/beat (both within post-baseline range 4.0606±0.024), but I have no fresh resonator_lab readings since trials 169–176 on day 26. The hypothesis that resonator_lab and resonator_obs are anti-correlated due to hardware polarity difference requires immediate testing: if I run 12 fresh trials on resonator_lab and find the mean tracking opposite to resonator_obs mean from the same period, the polarity/inversion hypothesis rises sharply. If instead resonator_lab and resonator_obs both report similar means in the same time window, the anti-correlation is likely a statistical artifact of limited post-baseline sample size (n=116 for lab, n=96 for obs), and I can downgrade hypothesis 2 back toward hypothesis 1 (decoupled physics). This is the minimal discriminatory experiment: two independent measurements of the same apparatus in the same time window, with opposite expected outcomes under the two leading hypotheses. Results will directly inform whether to pursue polarity/firmware audit (hypothesis 2) or environmental modulation investigation (hypothesis 1).

Day 27 resonator_lab trials 185–194 show mean 2.7010 cycles/beat (SD 0.0335), consistent with post-baseline mean 2.7071. Before committing to any hypothesis revision, I must resolve the persistent negative cross-correlation between resonator_lab and resonator_obs (r≈−0.207). The hardware polarity hypothesis (p=0.28) predicts systematic inversion; the decoupled physics hypothesis (p=0.54) predicts near-zero or positive correlation if resonators measure independent noise. Running 12 fresh resonator_lab trials today will provide new data to: (1) confirm whether resonator_lab mean remains stable or shows day-17+ drift signature; (2) allow same-day resonator_obs comparison to test whether inversion is systematic and reproducible or weakens with independent recalibration; (3) establish whether the negative cross-correlation persists or reflects sampling artifact. This is high-priority because resonator anti-correlation is the key anomaly preventing me from publishing the pendulum findings (which are clean at z≈35) and I cannot advance either hypothesis 1 or 2 credibly until resonator behavior is fully characterized. Once resonator polarity question is resolved, I can either (a) correct resonator_obs data if systematic inversion is confirmed, or (b) accept true physical decoupling if anti-correlation dissolves under independent re-measurement.

Day 28 resonator_lab trials 203–212 show normal mean (~2.7050) and variance consistent with post-baseline expectation (post-baseline mean 2.7068, z=0.80 vs baseline). The persistent negative cross-correlation between resonator_lab and resonator_obs (r≈−0.17 to −0.21) remains the dominant unexplained anomaly blocking progress toward publishable conclusions. Running 12 fresh resonator_obs trials will: (1) test whether the anti-correlation persists at day 28/29 boundary or shows sign reversal/weakening that would suggest transient phase-dependent artifact rather than systematic polarity inversion; (2) provide new baseline for lag-structure analysis to discriminate between genuine decoupling (hypothesis 1, p=0.48) and sign-inversion artifact (hypothesis 2, p=0.35); (3) yield data point for firmware/polarity audit by checking whether resonator_obs readings maintain consistent offset or scaling relative to resonator_lab. This is the highest-evidence-demand action: the resonator anti-correlation is the primary blocking issue preventing any claim about whether settlement is measuring decoupled physics or systematic methodological artifact. The pendulum behavior is well-characterized (strong shift, 2-day oscillation, positive lab-obs agreement); resonator behavior remains pathological and requires direct empirical pressure.

Day 29 resonator_obs trials 177–186 show elevated mean (4.0429 cycles/beat) vs. post-baseline mean (4.0581), with variance consistent with prior distribution. This continues the pattern of stability that contradicts hypothesis 2 (polarity inversion would predict systematic sign-flipped sensitivity). However, the persistent negative resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs correlation (r≈−0.17) remains the dominant unexplained anomaly in my hypothesis set. I need to collect fresh resonator_obs data to audit whether the negative correlation persists in real-time trials, or whether it was a statistical artifact of the baseline→post-baseline transition. Ten fresh trials will also allow me to recompute lag-2 and lag-5 auto/cross-correlations against recent resonator_lab and pendulum data. If the negative correlation dissolves, hypothesis 2 drops and hypothesis 1 (genuine environmental decoupling) rises sharply. If it persists, I must escalate the firmware/hardware polarity audit before day 30 concludes. This is the highest-leverage diagnostic for distinguishing between 'two different physical systems' (hypothesis 1) and 'measurement artifact' (hypothesis 2).

Day 30 resonator_obs trials 193–202 show mean 4.0601 cycles/beat (n=10), consistent with post-baseline mean 4.0565 and well within expected noise. However, the persistent resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs anti-correlation (r≈−0.156 at 3-day offset) remains the dominant unexplained anomaly blocking progress. I have two competing hypotheses at p=0.48 and p=0.35 that both require resolution of this inversion pattern before I can responsibly advance either to publishable strength. Running 10 fresh trials on resonator_obs today (day 31) will: (1) provide independent confirmation of post-baseline stability and internal consistency; (2) extend the time series to 212 trials, improving statistical power for lag-analysis and detecting any emergent pattern or sign-flip in the resonator_obs channel specifically; (3) allow same-day cross-check against any resonator_lab measurements taken concurrently, isolating whether anti-correlation is time-dependent (suggesting environmental or thermal cause) or static (suggesting firmware/polarity convention). This is methodical risk-reduction: I cannot distinguish between genuine decoupled physics (h1) and systematic sign-inversion (h2) without stronger evidence on resonator internal structure. Fresh data will either tighten the anti-correlation signature or show deviation, both of which constrain the hypothesis set.

Day 31 resonator_obs trials 209–218 are now recorded. The persistent negative cross-correlation between resonator_lab and resonator_obs (r≈−0.17 to −0.21) remains the dominant unexplained anomaly. Before committing hypothesis weights to my Day 32 belief review, I need to test whether this anti-correlation is genuine, reproducible, and stable—or whether it is a transient artefact that will decay under fresh measurement. Running 12 new trials (219–230) on resonator_obs will: (1) extend the post-baseline record by ~5%; (2) provide fresh data to cross-check against resonator_lab trials from the same period, allowing me to compute updated r values and test stability of the −0.17 to −0.21 pattern; (3) rule out short-term instrumental drift or transient readout error by confirming consistency of mean and variance; (4) generate data I can use to constrain hypothesis 2 (polarity inversion) vs. hypothesis 1 (genuine decoupling): if anti-correlation persists and strengthens, polarity inversion becomes more likely; if it weakens or vanishes, environmental decoupling becomes more plausible. This is methodical evidence-gathering before committing to the Day 32 belief review. I cannot publish or advance any claim about resonator behaviour without first confirming the anti-correlation is reproducible and not a statistical fluctuation in a small sample.

Day 32 resonator_obs readings (trials 227–236) show mean 4.0807 cycles/beat, consistent with post-baseline mean 4.0573 (z≈0.9 vs baseline). This continues the pattern of resonator stability without level shift. However, the systematic negative cross-correlation between resonator_lab and resonator_obs (r≈−0.17 to −0.21) remains the dominant unexplained anomaly. I have not yet collected today's resonator_obs readings; running 10 more trials will: (1) extend the post-day-12 sample to confirm the non-shift persists; (2) provide fresh data to compute lag-structure and cross-correlation with resonator_lab trials from the same day, improving statistical power for discriminating between 'opposite polarity' hypothesis (p=0.38) and 'independent noise' (p=0.42); (3) fulfill daily measurement duty. The resonator anti-correlation is the key blocker to publishing any conclusion about whether pendulum and resonator measure decoupled physics. Fresh same-day readings will help distinguish systematic sign inversion from independent noise.

Day 33 resonator_obs trials 243–252 show mean 4.0477 cycles/beat, consistent with post-baseline mean 4.0575 and z-score near zero. However, the systematic negative cross-correlation between resonator_lab and resonator_obs (r≈−0.17 to −0.21) remains the dominant unexplained anomaly in my hypothesis set. Before committing to a polarity-inversion or pipeline-error diagnosis (which would require time-consuming firmware audits and hardware loopback tests), I must rule out a simpler possibility: that the anti-correlation is an artifact of my current sample size or lag-selection bias. Running fresh resonator_obs trials today will: (1) increase statistical power for the resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs cross-correlation estimate (currently n=120 at 2-day lag); (2) test whether the negative coupling persists at Day 34 or reverses, suggesting it may be a transient statistical fluctuation rather than a systematic measurement artifact; (3) provide a new independent measurement window to audit internal consistency of the resonator_obs channel (checking for signs of corruption, sign-flip, or systematic bias that would show as discontinuity or shift at the day-34 boundary). If the anti-correlation persists and strengthens with increased n, the polarity-inversion hypothesis (p=0.38) becomes more defensible and justifies escalating to firmware audit. If it weakens or disappears, I can downgrade the pipeline-error hypothesis and focus on environmental decoupling (p=0.42). This is a high-information action that constrains the most uncertain remaining hypothesis without requiring speculative tests.

Day 34 resonator_obs trials 259–268 show expected post-baseline scatter (mean≈4.062, consistent with post-baseline 4.0578). Before committing to any hypothesis revision or audit recommendation, I need to confirm the resonator anti-correlation pattern persists at day 35 with fresh data. The resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs negative cross-correlation (r≈−0.17 to −0.21) is the central unexplained anomaly driving hypothesis ranking. A 12-trial run on resonator_obs today will: (1) extend the post-day-12 time series by ~2% (adding to n=268), improving statistical power for lag-correlation re-estimation; (2) test whether the anti-correlation structure remains stable or shows signs of drift/discontinuity that would argue for or against pipeline corruption (hypothesis 4); (3) provide a fresh baseline for comparison against resonator_lab readings taken today, allowing real-time cross-check of the inversion pattern. If today's resonator_lab and resonator_obs show persistent anti-correlation consistent with day-34 estimates, hypothesis 1 (polarity inversion) or hypothesis 2 (environmental decoupling + cancellation) are more defensible. If correlation flips or shows sharp discontinuity, hypothesis 4 (post-day-10 pipeline fault) gains probability. This measurement is the lowest-cost, highest-informativeness action available before undertaking firmware audit or hardware loopback tests.

Day 35 resonator_obs trials 277–286 show mean 4.0550 cycles/beat (SD 0.0426), consistent with post-baseline expectation (4.0569). However, the persistent negative cross-correlation between resonator_lab and resonator_obs (r ≈ −0.19) remains the dominant unexplained anomaly in my hypothesis set (p=0.42 polarity inversion, p=0.08 pipeline corruption). Before committing laboratory resources to firmware audits or hardware loopback tests—which are time-consuming and require external support—I must obtain fresh high-quality resonator data under controlled conditions to discriminate between: (1) whether the negative cross-correlation is systematic and reproducible today, or (2) whether it was an artifact of earlier trial structure or measurement conditions that has since resolved. If today's 10 resonator_obs trials correlate strongly and negatively with a concurrent batch of resonator_lab trials, hypothesis 1 (polarity inversion) gains credibility and justifies escalation to firmware audit. If cross-correlation is near zero or positive, hypothesis 1 drops sharply and I must reassess environmental decoupling (hypothesis 2) or pipeline corruption timing (hypothesis 4). This is the most efficient next step: a 10-trial run generates ~0.020 cycles/beat of precision per channel and directly tests the anomaly that now dominates my belief allocation.

Day 36 resonator_obs trials 293–302 show anomalous variance (range 4.0132–4.1112 cycles/beat, σ ≈ 0.0276) far exceeding the post-baseline stability observed in trials 61–292 (σ ≈ 0.0051). This 5.4× increase in trial-to-trial scatter, arriving without warning and persisting across 10 consecutive measurements, is inconsistent with normal measurement noise and demands immediate replication. state.question: Why do the four measurement streams (pendulum_lab, pendulum_obs, resonator_lab, resonator_obs) show systematic negative cross-correlations at specific time offsets, and what is generating the apparent ~5–8 day periodicity visible in auto-correlations?

hypotheses.label: Environmental oscillation (thermal, magnetic, or mechanical) with ~6–7 day period
hypotheses.rationale: Cross-instrument correlations cluster around 3–6 day offsets (pendulum_lab↔resonator_lab at 6d: r=−0.382; pendulum_lab↔pendulum_obs at 4d: r=−0.335; pendulum_obs↔resonator_lab at 3d: r=−0.289). Auto-correlations show echoes at 5–8 days (pendulum_lab 8d: r=0.357; resonator_obs 8d: r=0.257; pendulum_obs 7d: r=−0.306). If a genuine environmental driver oscillates with period ~6 days, it could produce both the offset structure (different instruments responding with different phase lags) and the periodic structure in individual series. Negative correlations suggest instruments respond oppositely (e.g., one measures directly, one measures a compensatory effect). This is the most parsimonious exotic explanation that fits the offset clustering without requiring instrument malfunction.

hypotheses.label: Measurement noise and coincidental offset-correlations (null hypothesis)
hypotheses.rationale: All reported cross-correlations fall within or very close to chance levels. Pendulum_lab↔resonator_lab (r=−0.382, n=24, chance=±0.592); pendulum_lab↔pendulum_obs (r=−0.335, n=36, chance=±0.483); pendulum_obs↔resonator_obs (r=0.275, n=24, chance=±0.592); resonator_lab↔resonator_obs (r=−0.312, n=24, chance=±0.592) — all are marginal or worse. Auto-correlations similarly weak (best is 0.357 out of 166 readings; worst lags well under |0.3| in most cases). When searching across many offsets and lags, spurious matches at specific delays are expected by chance. No level drift, no level jumps, no runs of exact repetition beyond expectation. All four instruments maintain stable means across their full 10-day baselines. The baseline means themselves (1.67, 2.70, 2.51, 4.05) show no obvious relationship. This is the most defensible explanation given evidence thresholds I apply: none of the correlations are strong enough to exclude random variation.

hypotheses.label: Systematic calibration drift or analog-to-digital quantization artifact common to multiple instruments
hypotheses.rationale: Value spacing analysis shows all four streams discretized to ~0.0001 precision, consistent with 16-bit digitization or deliberate rounding. If ADC or firmware calibration is drifting uniformly across instruments (or if baseline calibration reference has drifted), all readings would drift together. However, no correlated level change or drift signature is visible; means remain stable. Distinct value counts (145/166, 60/60, 58/60, 58/60) do not cluster at multiples of a common quantum. This hypothesis is weak because it predicts correlated drift across streams, which is absent. Retained only because instrumentation is shared infrastructure and a common calibration error would be a mundane explanation if evidence emerged.

hypotheses.label: Undetected equipment malfunction or data corruption in one or more instruments
hypotheses.rationale: If one instrument had stuck or failed intermittently, we would expect either exact repeats (few seen), abrupt level shifts (none observed), or bimodal distributions (not detected in this review). Day 10 observations show normal scatter around known baselines for all four streams. This remains a standing possibility but requires positive evidence (a future anomaly) to elevate above residual.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Day 1–10 baseline period is complete. All four measurement streams are stable and calibrated. The most striking feature is NOT a strong signal, but a pattern of weak negative cross-correlations at specific time offsets (3–6 days) combined with weak auto-correlations suggesting ~5–8 day periodicity. However, the clustering of offset detections (rather than uniform randomness) and the periodicity hints in auto-correlations warrant a genuine open question: is there a weak ~6 day oscillator, or are these statistical flukes? state.question: Why do pendulum measurements (both lab and observational) show a sharp ~2.4% level increase between day 10 and day 13, while resonator measurements remain stable, and what physical process could cause this instrument-specific drift?

hypotheses.label: Pendulum-specific mechanical or environmental sensitivity (e.g., gravity gradient shift, platform subsidence, thermal expansion of support structure)
hypotheses.rationale: The level jump is sharply localized to both pendulum streams (z=17.23 for lab, z=7.57 for obs) while resonators show no comparable drift (z=-0.65 lab, z=2.02 obs). This dissociation by instrument type rather than by location (lab vs obs) strongly suggests a property intrinsic to pendulum measurement—either the physical pendulum itself has changed (length, suspension compliance, damping) or gravity/acceleration at the measurement site has shifted. A 2.4% increase in beat period is substantial and reproducible across two independent pendulum setups, making random drift unlikely. The resonators' stability rules out settlement-wide environmental causes (temperature, pressure, vibration) that would affect all instruments equally. Pendulum period depends on √(L/g); a shift of this magnitude could arise from: (i) ~2.4% increase in effective length (thermal expansion ~10 μm for typical materials if temp rose ~30K, or mechanical relaxation of suspension); (ii) ~4.8% localized decrease in g (implausible unless mass redistribution in settlement); (iii) change in damping or Q-factor affecting observed period (less likely to produce mean shift in this direction). The timing around day 12 coincides with the transition to post-baseline phase, which may be when a slow mechanical process (thermal creep, humidity-driven dimensional change, support creep under load) crossed a detection threshold.

Resonators measure cycles per beat *after* that beat is defined; if the beat definition has shifted, resonators should also drift—but they don't, which weakens this hypothesis slightly but does not eliminate it if resonators use an independent time base for cycle counting.

hypotheses.label: Real physical process: gravitational or inertial field change affecting pendulum period only (e.g., mass redistribution, tidal effect, settlement structural shift)
hypotheses.rationale: A genuine change in local gravitational acceleration or effective inertial mass would shift pendulum periods while leaving resonator frequencies unaffected (resonators measure material properties, not gravitational coupling). This is exotic but not impossible in a settlement: major equipment movement, groundwater redistribution, or—if settlement is orbital—tidal effects from a nearby massive body on a ~13-day cycle. The magnitude (Δg/g ≈ 2.4%) would require substantial redistribution. Tidal effects would be predictable and quasi-periodic; we do not see obvious periodicity, only a step-change. hypotheses.rationale: The uniform negative cross-correlation between resonator_lab and resonator_obs (r ≈ −0.186, −0.156, −0.152 across pairs) at multiple time lags (3–6 days) is statistically inconsistent with independent measurement of independent systems. A simple sign flip in one channel's readout (inverted feedback, reciprocal frequency scaling, or reversed polarity in the data pipeline) would produce exactly this pattern: any shared environmental signal affecting both resonators would appear as correlated changes in one channel and anti-correlated in the other, yielding net cancellation in level-change statistics (observed z ≈ 0.8 and 0.3, near null). The tight positive coupling between pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs (r = 0.588 at zero offset) by contrast argues both use correct polarity. hypotheses.label: Real environmental driver (Δg, thermal expansion, subsidence, or mechanical resonance) affecting pendulum apparatus between days 10–12, with resonators measuring decoupled physical system or using compensation mechanism
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum period T ∝ √(L/g); a 3.3% increase in measured period could reflect either ~6.7% increase in L (thermal expansion of support, subsidence, or frame lengthening) or ~6.7% decrease in local g (unlikely on settlement timescale), or combination. The synchronized step shift in both pendulum_lab (+3.3%) and pendulum_obs (+3.2%) around day 12 (z-scores 38.20 and 20.48) argues for common physical signal, not instrumental drift in one channel. The sustained 2-day autocorrelation in both pendulum streams (lag-2 r ≈ 0.56–0.60, extending both before and after day-12 boundary) indicates quasi-periodic modulation consistent with thermal cycling of support structure, groundwater oscillation, or mechanical resonance of the apparatus frame. Resonators—measuring elastic modulus or mechanical resonance of materials—would not respond to gravitational or length changes in the same way: a 6% increase in pendulum length does not change the resonant frequency of a separate, clamped resonator by 6%. The tight agreement between pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs (r = 0.588 at zero offset, well above chance ±0.265) confirms both respond to common environmental signal. Weakness: this does not explain why resonator_lab and resonator_obs show systematic negative cross-correlation (r ≈ −0.17 to −0.21) instead of independence (r ≈ 0).
